_why: Cross-engine vectors for the secret rules that are not tied to one vendor.
Same shape and same contract as vendor_probes.json in this directory, and
read by the same two harnesses: tools/run_tests.sh pushes every string here
through Python, web/tools/parity.mjs pushes the same strings through V8.
A SIBLING FILE RATHER THAN MORE ROWS IN vendor_probes.json. That file is
named for the eight vendor-prefix rules added 2026-08-31 and its _why is
written about them. A password assignment is not a vendor prefix, and a
vector filed under a name that does not describe it is a vector the next
person does not find when they change the rule it belongs to.
WHY BOTH ENGINES READ ONE FILE. web/tools/parity.mjs compares regex SOURCE
and flags, never behaviour, so two engines can hold byte-identical patterns
and still disagree on a string. That is ROW-109 and
record/findings/parity-compares-regex-source-not-behaviour.md. Feeding one
set of strings through both is the only check that can see it. A vector
added here is checked in both engines or in neither.
These live in tools/fixtures/ because that is the one path .gitleaks.toml
allowlists for deliberately fake credentials. Do not move them into a file
that holds real code, and do not widen the allowlist to follow them.
Every string below is synthetic. None is or ever was a live credential.
must_fire is single-line ONLY. run_tests.sh asserts that scrub.py redacts
every must_fire vector under a NAMED rule, and scrub.py applies its named
rules per line, so a vector spanning a newline cannot satisfy that
assertion however correct the rule is. The wrapped-password vectors live in
the PROBES list in web/tools/parity.mjs instead, which compares preflight
against the endpoint and scans whole bodies on both sides.
THREE GROUPS, NOT TWO. must_fire must trip a rule, must_not_fire must trip
none, and known_false_positives must ALSO trip a rule. The third group is
not a wish list. It holds strings that are ordinary content and that the
password rule refuses anyway, pinned so that a change which silently starts
or stops refusing one of them fails the gate instead of passing it. They
moved out of must_not_fire on 2026-09-03 when the union landed; every one
of them is refused by the rule that ships on main today, so this is a
record of live behaviour and not a new cost. Both harnesses read all three
groups. If you fix one of these, move it back to must_not_fire in the same
commit.

must_fire._note: Every one of these was published by both gates before 2026-09-01. ROW-131 item 1.
must_fire._note_unchanged: Caught before this rewrite too. Here so a later narrowing cannot pass unseen.
must_fire._note_punctuation: Passwords contain punctuation, and an earlier version of this rule counted the first three characters with a class that excluded ! $ backtick comma semicolon and brackets, so every one of these was missed. Two of them were regressions against the rule this replaced. Found by a critic, 2026-09-01.
must_fire._note_engine: U+017F casefolds to s under Python's re.I and not under V8's /i. Main's rule carries re.I, so preflight refused this and the endpoint PUBLISHED it, which is the direction that leaks. This rule carries no case flag in either engine, so against THIS rule the long s is a recall gap rather than a divergence; the parity story is true of main's. The trigger classes spell it out as [Ssſ], written here as the letter class rather than the character, so neither engine depends on case folding and both fire. Measured over 119,837 third-party files: widening the classes changed nothing, +0 files and +0 occurrences. If these two ever disagree again, the engines have split.
must_fire._note_bare_keyword: The four bare trigger words with no prefix. Three fire and one does not, and that asymmetry is the rule's design rather than an oversight: password, passwd and pwd are credential words on their own, and pass is not, so the weak arm requires a separator or a preceding lowercase before it. Bare pass sits in must_not_fire.
must_fire._note_composite: ROW-131 item 1 landed as three repairs, not one. Each of the next groups is one of them, and each was published by both gates before 2026-09-03.
must_fire._note_backtick: A backticked value. The optional delimiter around the assignment accepted a double or single quote and not a backtick, so a template literal walked past the whole rule. Corpus cost of accepting it: +2 occurrences and +0 files in 119,837.
must_fire._note_vocabulary: A password that BEGINS with a placeholder word is not a placeholder. The vocabulary guard's tail used to run over digits and underscores, so any real password with a placeholder-shaped first syllable was released. The tail is now letters and hyphens only: a placeholder word counts when the whole value is words. Whole-value placeholders are still released and sit in must_not_fire.
must_fire._note_pin: The pure-digit guard was unbounded, so a numeric PIN of any length was read as a port number. It is bounded to seven digits now. A port, a timeout and a five-digit id stay released; an eight-digit PIN is a password.
must_fire._note_bare_value_lead: The regression ROW-131's first cut introduced lived entirely here, and the suite had no probe in the region. Every password vector above uses a PREFIXED keyword (db_password, smtpPass, DB_PASSWORD), where \b cannot fire and the value-side exclusions decide. On a BARE password the exclusions are what a high-entropy value collides with: a leading bracket, a leading slash, an early quote. These four are the shapes measured to leak at 15.28% of 1Password-style generated passwords. The My- twin above is filed under vocabulary; this one is filed under the bare keyword on purpose, because the two guards that release it are different guards.
must_fire.row-152: space-separated passphrase, pre: db_password: correct horse battery staple otter kettle
must_fire._note_whitespace_regression_2026_09_05: These two exist because a critic found the backstop arm's operator had regressed from \s* to [ \t]*(?:\r?\n[ \t]*)*, silently dropping NBSP, other Unicode spaces, U+2028/2029, bare CR, VT, FF and U+001C-001F -- codepoints a pasted config line from Word, Notion, Confluence or a rendered web page can carry. Fixed by restoring \s* on both sides of the operator; these two probes are the source-level tripwire the fix needed and did not have, so a future re-narrowing of this operator goes red here without needing a corpus fuzz to find it. See record/findings/row-150-151-152-cross-product-gaps-and-the-backstop-arm.md.

must_not_fire._note: Ordinary content. A gate that refuses these turns away a stranger who cannot see the rule.
must_not_fire._note_labels: The next two are released by their VALUE, not by their name. Verified: bypass and minipass in front of an ordinary strong value both fire. The trigger does not release an identifier ending in pass, and whoever next changes the trigger should not read these as evidence that it does.
must_not_fire._note_bare_pass: Bare pass with nothing in front of it. The weak arm needs a separator or a preceding lowercase, because pass on its own is an ordinary English word and a test status.
must_not_fire._note_orphaned_guards_2026_09_05: Five notes removed here on 2026-09-05 (a critic caught them): each described a guard -- the shell-variable exclusion's ${...}/$UPPER_NAME bound, the <angle-bracket> placeholder spelling, the whole-value-is-a-placeholder release, the bounded-digit release -- whose probe had since moved to known_false_positives as a prefixed twin (ROW-151 removed the bare/prefixed asymmetry these probes were testing). A note describing a guard whose probe no longer lives here was annotating nothing. The guards themselves are unchanged and still live in the WEAK ('pass') arm only; what changed is that the bare-keyword arm no longer shares them, so a probe built to show the guard releasing a BARE name now shows the STRONG/backstop arm firing instead, which is why it belongs in known_false_positives now, not here. The shell-variable guard is still exercised as a true negative in this file by 'a bypass identifier, released by the shell-variable guard' below; the version-range guard by 'an npm version range, released by the version guard'. The placeholder, whole-value-placeholder and bounded-digit guards have no remaining must_not_fire probe on the weak arm as of this commit -- they are exercised only implicitly, by fixtures/scrub_false_positives.md and by their prefixed known_false_positives twins. That is a real gap, not hidden: adding a weak-arm probe for each (e.g. `bypass = your-example-here` for the placeholder guard) is open work, not done in this commit.

known_false_positives._note: Ordinary content that the password rule refuses. Every one of these is refused by the rule shipping on main today, so none is a regression; they sat in must_not_fire until 2026-09-03 because the first ROW-131 cut released them, and releasing them was the same value-side exclusion that leaked 15.28% of generated passwords on the bare keyword. The trade was taken deliberately: a bare password keyword followed by a separator and a non-space value is refused whatever the value looks like. Read the cost plainly. A hand-redacted file is still refused, so an owner who redacts a password themselves and uploads the result is turned away with the same message as an owner who did not. record/findings/the-union-password-rule-and-why-a-targeted-fix-fails.md holds the measurement. Do not repair one of these by adding a carve-out to the bare arm: the carve-out is matched against the value and a random value eventually matches it.
known_false_positives._note_bare_pwd: Found by fixtures/scrub_false_positives.md and not by this file, on 2026-09-03. must_not_fire already held a PWD probe, PWD": "/Users/someone", spelled with a quote before the colon, and that shape is released. A BARE PWD before a path is not, and the probe that was supposed to cover it did not. Two fixture files disagreeing is how this was seen at all; adding the shape here rather than only there is what makes it checked in both engines.
known_false_positives.a bare pwd before a path: Set PWD: "/Users/someone" before running the script.
known_false_positives._note_row151_prefixed_backstop_twins: Moved here 2026-09-05 (ROW-151) from must_not_fire. ROW-151 gave password/passwd/pwd a backstop arm with NO value-side exclusion on any prefix -- glued, separated, or none -- matching what main's own bare arm has always given the unprefixed form. Its operator keeps quote handling but drops the (?![=>~:]) guard the weak pass arm still carries; giving it the FULL guard was tried and reverted (it broke values starting with ~, =, > or :, which fixtures/password_rule_baseline.json exists to catch). Fifteen strings moved here: eight reached for the first time now that the backstop matches ANY prefix rather than only a bare keyword (withPassword, BSKY_APP_PASSWORD and the like were unreachable by any arm before ROW-151, since \b cannot fire between two letters and the weak pass arm never covers the full word password/passwd/pwd), and seven are the PREFIXED twin of an already-accepted bare false positive in this same group (password: {, password: dummy, password: 1234567, and so on), including 'if (a.db_password === b.db_password) {', whose bare twin has always fired here because main's own bare arm never guarded against ===. Verified against the corpus: 564 files fire where 477 did before, every one of the 87 new files traced to this cause or to the ROW-150 recall fixes below, zero files where the OLD rule fired and the new one does not. That corpus result does not cover every regression class: it caught none of the whitespace-operator narrowing a critic found the same day (NBSP and 24 other codepoints silently dropped from this arm's operator, fixed the same day the corpus numbers above were measured), because the corpus is npm/plugin text that cannot contain those codepoints next to this keyword. "Zero regressions" here means zero on this corpus, not zero, full stop. See record/findings/row-150-151-152-cross-product-gaps-and-the-backstop-arm.md.
